title: NY State Senate · District 21
area: Central and southeast Brooklyn (Flatbush, East Flatbush, Midwood, Flatlands, Mill Basin)

context.text: Both candidates advanced without a contested primary: Kevin Parker's Democratic primary and Ronald Seifert's Republican and Conservative Party primaries, all scheduled for June 23, 2026, were canceled for lack of an opponent.

Parker ran for New York City Comptroller in the 2025 Democratic primary and was eliminated in the second round of ranked-choice tabulation, receiving about 7.8% of the vote; Mark Levine won the primary and the general election.

summary.text: Kevin Parker is the incumbent Democratic state senator for District 21 in Brooklyn, in office since 2003. A longtime Flatbush resident, he worked in state and city government and taught at Brooklyn College before his election. He chairs the Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee, previously served as Majority Whip, ran unsuccessfully for New York City Comptroller in 2025, and is seeking re-election.

background.text: A lifelong Brooklyn resident who has lived in Flatbush for more than 31 years, according to his official Senate biography; attended New York City public schools including Midwood High School.

Earned a B.S. in public service from Pennsylvania State University (1989) and an M.S. from the New School for Social Research (1993); has been pursuing a Ph.D. in political science at the CUNY Graduate School and University Center.

Worked as a project manager for the New York State Urban Development Corporation, an instructor at Brooklyn College (1993-1997), a political action director for Paine Webber (1998-1999), and a special assistant in the Office of the New York State Comptroller (2000-2002).

Served as a legislative aide to New York City Council Member Una Clarke and as special assistant to Assemblyman Nick Perry; also worked as a special assistant to Manhattan Borough President Ruth Messinger and was a New York City Urban Fellow.
Ran for New York City Council in 2001 but was not elected, then won the State Senate seat and took office in 2003.

Chairs the Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee; also a member of the Banks, Civil Service and Pensions, Finance, Health, Internet and Technology, Judiciary, and Rules committees. Previously served as Senate Majority Whip.

According to his official bio, he founded the New York Ready Emergency Preparedness Unit, is First Vice Chair of the Association of Black, Puerto Rican & Asian Legislators, and was named a 2026 New York State Senate Veterans' Hall of Fame honoree.
Ran in the 2025 Democratic primary for New York City Comptroller and was eliminated in round 2 of the ranked-choice tabulation; Mark Levine won the general election.

positions.summary: Advocated for a higher minimum wage than the $8.75 rate then in effect, saying low-wage earners needed a wage they could actually live on.
positions.quote: Although $8.75 is a welcome start, it does not provide low-wage earners with a true minimum wage that they can live upon.

positions.summary: Supported continuing a higher state income-tax rate on millionaires, citing New Jersey data that higher earners taxed at a greater rate were not leaving the state.
positions.quote: studies from our neighboring state of New Jersey, where millionaires are taxed at a greater rate, have shown that the millionaires are not going to leave

positions.summary: Sponsored a tax-abatement bill for electric energy storage, describing it as a step toward a cleaner energy future for New York.
positions.quote: With the passage of my Tax Abatement Bill, we are taking a decisive step toward a cleaner, more resilient energy future for New York.

record.text: Sponsored S1329, which would direct utilities to limit residential fixed charges to costs directly tied to metering, billing, service connections, and customer service. It passed the Senate 46-14 in January 2025 and again 46-16 in February 2026; as of those votes it remained in the Assembly Energy Committee.
Sponsored S1330, establishing a statewide requirement that utility companies offer affordable payment plans to customers enrolled in social-service programs.

Sponsored S2011-A, directing the Department of State and the Public Service Commission to study utilities', cable companies', and cellphone carriers' disclosure of customers' late payments and defaults to credit-reporting agencies, with recommendations due by December 31, 2027.
Sponsored S3985, establishing a task force to study a state-issued cryptocurrency as a potential revenue source for New York; remained in the Senate Finance Committee as of January 2026.

In March 2011 was sentenced to three years' probation and fined $1,672 after being convicted of assaulting a New York Post photographer outside his home in a May 2009 incident in which he damaged the photographer's car and camera.
Chairs the Senate Energy and Telecommunications Committee in the 2025-2026 session.

summary.text: Ronald Seifert is the Republican and Conservative Party candidate challenging incumbent Kevin Parker. A lifelong Brooklyn resident and father of two, he has run a home contracting business for 18 years and has not previously held elected office. According to his campaign website, his priorities include lowering utility costs, public safety, fairer property taxes, and trade programs in public schools.

background.text: According to his campaign website, he is a lifelong Brooklyn resident and father of two, raised by a cab-driver father and a seamstress mother; his father served in the U.S. Army.
Attended P.S. 236 Mill Basin, J.H.S. 078 Roy H. Mann, and South Shore High School, and graduated from Kingsborough Community College.

Has owned and operated an NYC-licensed home contracting business for 18 years; earlier worked in transportation operations at Atlantic Express, in logistics for DHL at JFK, and for New York City through the Department of Citywide Administrative Services, and owned an auto repair and installation shop.

Volunteered with a local team during a Republican mayoral campaign; has not held elected office. Ballotpedia lists him as advancing from the June 23, 2026 Republican primary, which was canceled, and as the Conservative Party candidate.

A longtime Knights of Columbus member who has helped with food and clothing drives, school scholarships, donations for a local Catholic church, and interfaith service with Catholic and Jewish neighbors.

priorities.text: Push for stronger state oversight, transparency, and accountability to lower utility costs
Support measures for safer streets and neighborhood quality of life
Fight for property tax relief for one- and two-family homeowners
Require community input, safety planning, and accountability review before siting homeless or migrant shelters
Advocate stricter safety standards for battery storage facilities sited near homes and schools, and bring career and technical education back to schools

researchNotes: Neither candidate has completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey. Ronald Seifert has never held office, so he has no official voting or legislative record; his platform (utility costs, public safety, property taxes, shelter siting, battery-storage safety, and career/technical education) does not map cleanly onto this guide's fixed issue list, so no positions are recorded for him -- see his priorities for his stated views in his own words. Kevin Parker's campaign website was not located; his biography draws on his official Senate page and Ballotpedia. Seifert's biography relies mainly on his own campaign site, so its details are self-described.
